# The Mechanical Logic: How a Coin Disables Central Locking

Recent warnings from law enforcement agencies highlight a disturbing shift in automotive theft tactics. Thieves are no longer solely relying on high-end electronic hacking tools or relay attacks to bypass security; they are exploiting a fundamental design flaw inherent in many legacy central locking systems. The method involves inserting a simple 5-cent coin into the passenger door handle while the vehicle is locked and driving away. Upon stopping, the driver attempts to lock the car again, only to find the system unresponsive. This leaves the interior accessible from the outside immediately upon opening any door, effectively bypassing the primary security layer without ever needing to touch the ignition or the electronic control unit (ECU).

To understand why this works, we must look at the architecture of standard power window and central locking assemblies found in vehicles manufactured before the widespread adoption of CAN bus integration for these specific functions. In many older architectures, the door handles are not merely passive mechanical levers; they act as switches that signal the Body Control Module (BCM) or a dedicated Central Locking Relay to engage the solenoids on all four doors simultaneously.

The critical vulnerability lies in how these systems interpret the "lock" command versus the physical state of the handle. When you insert a coin into the slot, you are mechanically engaging the internal latch mechanism that triggers the door-open signal. However, because the coin is wedged inside, it prevents the return spring from resetting the handle to its neutral, closed position.

When the BCM or locking relay receives a request to lock the vehicleâusually triggered by turning off the ignition or pressing a central buttonâit first polls the status of every door loop. If any door reports an "open" state via its switch, the logic dictates that the system must not engage the locks to prevent trapping someone inside. The coin holds the handle in a position where the microswitch detects the lever is depressed or moving, mimicking a door being actively opened or held ajar.

This creates a false positive for the central locking algorithm. The system assumes the interior is compromised because it detects an active latch state on the passenger side. Consequently, the command to engage the solenoids is ignored or explicitly blocked by a safety check designed to prevent accidental locking while a door is "open." The result is that the doors remain unlocked, yet the driver believes they are secure.

From an engineering perspective, this highlights the danger of relying exclusively on state flags without verifying physical continuity or position via redundant sensors. A robust implementation would involve independent verification mechanisms, such as optical encoders or dual-switch logic that confirms the handle has actually returned to the closed position before allowing a lock cycle.

For developers working on IoT security or embedded systems with physical interfaces, this serves as a stark reminder of the attack surface provided by legacy hardware protocols. It demonstrates how a minimal inputâmechanical obstructionâcan trivialize a complex electronic safety logic. Modern vehicles have largely mitigated this risk by integrating door handle sensors into the CAN bus network, allowing the ECU to read precise position data rather than relying on simple limit switches that can be mechanically fooled. However, for any system maintaining legacy hardware, adding a secondary verification step is essential to prevent exactly this kind of mechanical bypass.
